subject: chemistry
question_text: Why is the gas constant R called the universal gas constant?

verification.note: Chapter 4 (States of Matter) is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.62-66), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The book prints NO Long Answer section for this chapter, so no 8-mark form is invented. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The book lists R = 0.0821 L atm and 1.987 cal values; this card adds the SI value 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, which the book itself uses in its SAQ 8 answer.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The reason
lines: In PV = nRT the constant R has the same value
for ALL gases, whatever their nature — hydrogen,
Because its value does not depend on the gas,
R is called the universal gas constant.
steps.why: The van der Waals constants a and b change from gas to gas, but R does not. Same value for every gas is exactly what the word universal claims, so the reason must state that independence.
common_mistakes: Saying R is constant at all temperatures. The point is that it is the same for all GASES.
Quoting values without stating the reason. The why carries its own mark.
steps.memory_tip: Universal = same for every gas. Contrast with a and b, which are different for every gas.
steps.margin_note: The phrase same for all gases must appear in the sentence.

steps.label: The values
steps.why: One constant, three unit systems: joules for SI work, litre-atmospheres for gas-law problems in atm and L, calories for energy written in the older calorie unit. All three describe the same R.
common_mistakes: Attaching the wrong unit to a value, such as 0.0821 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Writing 8.314 with no unit at all.
steps.memory_tip: Match the size to the unit: 8.314 goes with J, 0.0821 with L atm, about 2 with cal.
steps.margin_note: Any one value with its correct unit earns the mark; the three together are the safe answer.

insider_note: The mark is in the pairing of number and unit — examiners see 0.0821 with J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ every year and it earns nothing.
